leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: Old Medical School
description: This vast red sandstone complex, designed by Robert Rowand Anderson after he won an 1874 architectural competition, opened through the 1880s in a Northern Italian Renaissance style, with palazzo-style frontages and a corbelled stair turret. It was built to give Edinburgh's rapidly growing Medical School - founded back in 1726 and previously squeezed into Old College - room to expand, and its footprint is enormous: the complex runs the entire length of the block from Teviot Place down the top of Middle Meadow Walk. Integral to the new building was a purpose-built Anatomical Museum, which opened in 1884 and still holds the university's historic anatomy and pathology collections today. The courtyard at its heart was officially renamed the Elsie Inglis Quadrangle in 2017, and its walls are lined with blue plaques to the school's most influential figures.
interesting_fact: Along the quad's walls: Sir James Young Simpson, who discovered chloroform's anaesthetic properties in 1847 after testing it on himself one evening; Joseph Lister, whose antiseptic techniques transformed surgical survival rates; Sir Robert Sibbald, the school's 17th-century founding professor; James Lind, whose 1747 trial proved citrus cured scurvy; Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, a medical graduate who based Sherlock Holmes's deductive method on one of his own professors here; physiologist Sir Edward Sharpey-Schafer, a pioneer of hormone research; and three trailblazing women - Sophia Jex-Blake, one of the 'Edinburgh Seven' who fought to open medical education to women; Elsie Inglis, the WWI medical pioneer the quadrangle is now named after; and Mary Pickford, who became the school's first female professor in 1966.

name: George Heriot's School (Main Building)
description: George Heriot, court goldsmith and moneylender to James VI known popularly as 'Jinglin' Geordie', left just over £23,625 on his death in 1624 - worth several million pounds today - to found a charitable hospital school for 'poor fatherless bairns'. Its foundation stone was laid in 1628, with master mason William Wallace leading construction until his death in 1631, succeeded by William Aytoun and then John Mylne; Sir William Bruce later added the distinctive central tower between 1676 and 1693. Building work was interrupted when Oliver Cromwell's occupying troops used the half-finished quadrangle as a barracks, reportedly stabling horses in what would become the chapel. It finally opened in 1659 with thirty pupils, converted to a fee-paying day school in 1885, and admitted girls for the first time in 1979.
interesting_fact: Generations of pupils have nicknamed the building 'the Wark' - simply 'the works' - out of grudging local affection for what is widely considered one of the finest examples of Scottish Renaissance architecture anywhere in the country. Its quadrangle also holds the more sombre distinction of having been the first large building constructed outside Edinburgh's old town walls.

leg: McEwan Hall -> Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
name: Middle Meadow Walk
address: Middle Meadow Walk, Edinburgh (northern end, near Teviot Place)
description: This tree-lined path began taking shape in 1722, when Thomas Hope of Rankeillor leased the old, boggy bed of the drained Burgh Loch and set about turning it into an ornamental park with formal walkways. In 1737 the Town Council granted a strip of land across George Heriot's Hospital's own grounds to extend the route north toward Forrest Road, and it opened fully to the public in 1743 once a gap was cut through the old city wall at its head. It was formally relaid in the 1850s after a Town Council design competition, gaining stone bollards and ornamental pillars topped with carved unicorns in place of its original wooden posts.
interesting_fact: For roughly 170 years, Edinburgh's civic authorities and residents fought off repeated attempts to open this route to wheeled traffic - documented campaigns in 1864, 1871, 1873-74, 1876, 1879, 1885, 1892, 1895, 1915, 1919, 1921-22, 1928, 1931, 1935-36, 1946 and 1962 all failed, several defeated by public meetings thousands strong. The only concession ever won was a cycle lane added in 1983, meaning this has remained a pedestrian route in substance for very nearly three centuries.
